source.title: Generalization Through The Lens Of Leave-One-Out Error
source.authors: Gregor Bachmann; Thomas Hofmann; Aurélien Lucchi

record.tranche_reason: The study tests double-descent behavior using finite-dimensional random-feature models and kernel methods, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper also plots leave-one-out quantities alongside test quantities to assess LOO as a generalization proxy; the rows below record the test metrics relevant to the claim. Values in the cited figures are not transcribed in the text. The paper discusses other works' findings, which are not recorded as results here.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own test-loss curves over random-feature width on binary MNIST. Test loss spikes at the interpolation threshold (m* ≈ n), which bears on V4 in a non-deep model class. The study's main aim is LOO as a generalization proxy, but the test-error results are its own.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that closed-form LOO loss and accuracy closely track test error for kernel-regime networks across sample size, label noise, width (double descent) and transfer learning. They also prove, under a Haar-rotation assumption, that ridgeless LOO loss spikes at the interpolation threshold and diverges as n grows. The 'broadly applicable' framing rests on that theorem and on one random-label experiment.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses kernel/NTK and random-feature formulations, and evaluates LOO alongside test metrics; its empirical width sweep is not a reproduction of the original deep-network training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The critical interpolation width depends on the feature-map architecture; deeper random-feature models have more nuanced rank dynamics and thresholds that need not coincide with sample count.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 4.3 (Haar-rotation assumption): at the interpolation point, LOO loss ≈ 2nA with A ~ Gamma(1/2,1), so it diverges as n grows. This concerns LOO, not measured test error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The height of the interpolation-threshold spike in (LOO) loss grows with sample size under ridgeless kernel regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix C.1: for depth-2 random features and linearization kernels, the kernel reaches full rank (interpolation) at widths other than m=n. Only rank is shown, not test-error peaks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The location of the interpolation threshold, and hence the double-descent peak, depends on feature-map architecture rather than raw parameter count.

record.problems: The main width-sweep metrics are shown in figures without numerical values in the text. The empirical double-descent width sweep uses a random-feature model on binary MNIST, and the theorem relies on a Haar-distributed rotation assumption. The label-noise width experiment uses fully randomized labels rather than a sweep over noise levels.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant test results omitted. LOO proxy curves and figures about kernel rank were not separately recorded because the rows focus on test error or accuracy.

untested.parts: No deep-network width sweep; only random-feature models and infinite-width NTK are used.
No finite-capacity sample-size sweep near the interpolation threshold. The NTK sample sweeps are infinite width.
No single complexity measure is tested across axes. Appendix C.1 shows only kernel-rank thresholds, not test-error peaks.
Noise level is not varied in the width sweep, and there are no regularization-tuning or multiple-peak test-error results.
Only 1-layer random-feature models on binary MNIST are tested. There is no test-error width sweep for deeper random features or the linearization kernels.

missing.what: Train loss curve over width, showing where interpolation is reached relative to the test-loss spike

record.verdict_notes: r1–r4 do not concern double descent and are relinked to none. The reader's V4 limits_scope label from r8 is removed, because chance-level accuracy under random labels is expected and uninformative. The V6 support label is removed, because noise dependence is not isolated. The random-feature model is a different model class from deep networks, so the result bears on V4, not V1.

versions.untested_parts: The model-size sweep uses a random-feature model, not a deep network.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The sample-size experiments do not establish that the models are near an interpolation threshold.
Empirical model-size evidence is from random-feature models on binary MNIST; other model classes are not empirically tested.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The width sweep includes fully randomized labels, but does not systematically vary noise levels or test optimally tuned regularization, multiple peaks, or whether noise or variance causes the peak.
The paper does not show that measuring complexity by an effective parameter count converts the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

conditions.value: varying m; interpolation threshold around m* ≈ n

rows.note: The text states that test loss follows the LOO curve and exhibits a spike at the interpolation threshold.

rows.subject: random feature model
rows.operation_detail: Sweep feature width and measure test loss with fully randomized labels
rows.note: The text explicitly states that test loss has a strong spike around the interpolation threshold, even with fully randomized labels.
rows.check: Linking to V6 is unwarranted. The spike also appears with clean labels (r5, at a different n), and noise level is not varied, so noise dependence is not isolated.

rows.subject: random feature model
rows.operation_detail: Sweep feature width and measure test accuracy with fully randomized labels
rows.value: random guessing throughout all regimes of overparametrization
rows.note: The authors state that test accuracy shows no double-descent behavior and remains at random guessing.
rows.check: With fully random labels, test accuracy is necessarily at chance at every width. The authors call this expected, so this measure cannot show a double-descent shape. Not 'absent'.

relationships.condition: 1-layer ReLU random-feature model, ridgeless MSE, binary MNIST, n=5000 (clean labels) and n=2000 (random labels)
relationships.reason: Test loss spikes at the interpolation threshold m* ≈ n, with clean and with fully random labels (r5, r7); the second descent is read from the figure.
relationships.display_finding: Test loss spiked at m*≈n and then declined again for both clean and fully random labels.
